extracted.intended_audience: General public, students, educators, and anyone interested in Métis/Indigenous storytelling and cultural traditions
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and cultural standards for understanding, preserving, and respectfully retelling Métis oral-tradition stories — their forms, functions, characters, spiritual aspects, and social rules. Useful for storytellers, educators, and writers working with or about Métis narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-linear narrative structure
rubrics_metrics.description: All traditional Indigenous stories, including Métis ones, generally have non-linear narratives and, unlike European stories, many of them have no real beginning, middle or end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Métis stories are often ongoing and can be carried over through time; they do not follow a conventional linear plot arc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Layered meanings and multivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: The stories are layered and have multiple meanings, so people of varying ages will be left with different interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect and preserve ambiguity and multiple interpretive levels; stories can teach different lessons to children, adults, and Elders simultaneously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral and practical instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Valuable life lessons are taught in the Métis Oral Tradition (for instance, a story about gluttony may be told through a humorous Wiisakaychak trickster story).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories commonly encode ethical lessons and practical survival knowledge; maintain the instructional elements (morals, how-to knowledge) when retelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rooted in spirituality and creation narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: The Métis Oral Tradition is rooted in spirituality. Creation stories of how things came to be are usually told as trickster stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect and convey spiritual cosmologies; recognize trickster narratives often function as creation accounts and carry spiritual meaning and obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sacredness and restricted transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: Some narratives in the Oral Tradition are considered sacred and are told only at certain times, and only to specific people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume all stories may be publicly retold; ascertain which stories are restricted and follow cultural protocols about timing and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of traditional prayers and heritage languages
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional prayers and the giving of thanks in Métis heritage languages are handed down to families and are told only on very specific occasions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve and respect the role of original languages and ritual speech; recognize their situational use and sacred context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role in maintaining cosmologies and identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional Indigenous cosmologies are kept alive through the telling of these stories... The Métis Oral Tradition has retained a spiritual aspect from its Algonquian ancestral cultures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When engaging with stories, acknowledge their role in sustaining worldview, identity, and cultural continuity rather than treating them as mere entertainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinship, genealogy, and social regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Métis Oral Tradition has been important in delineating kinship networks and genealogies; before printed genealogies, oral records prevented close relatives from marrying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oral narratives often encode family ties, community boundaries, and social rules — these functions should be recognized and preserved in documentation or retelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transmission of practical ecological/foraging knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Narratives in the Oral Tradition taught where food was located, how to harvest it, and how to prepare and eat it (e.g., where to dig for wild turnips or the best time to hunt game animals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve practical, place-based information embedded in stories; such details are part of living knowledge systems and survival practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural hybridity and source traditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Métis stories seamlessly blend Cree, Ojibwa and French-Canadian traditions; a rural French/Catholic sphere and a Woodlands/Plains Algonquian sphere have been fused into one Métis storytelling tradition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge and represent the blended origins and distinct evolution of Métis stories rather than conflating them with any single source tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traditional character types and their narrative roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional Métis stories include tricksters (Wiisakaychak, Nanabush, Chi-Jean) who are essentially good characters with human foibles, as well as malevolent beings (Roogaroo, Whiitigo, Paakuk) and other entities (magical little people, lake monsters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray characters with their culturally specific roles: tricksters as creators/intermediaries who explain the natural world and teach lessons; malevolent beings to represent danger, discipline, or disease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morality enforcement and behavioral teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: Roogaroo (werewolf) or li Jiyaab (the Devil) stories are told so children do not forget their spiritual obligations to the Creator and to ensure that youth behaved themselves (e.g., during Lent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize stories as tools of socialization; maintain their prescriptive or cautionary functions when conveying them to new audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for storytellers and cultural protocols
rubrics_metrics.description: The Elder or storyteller who is sharing the story is doing so for a specific reason and not just for entertainment purposes. If you retell a Métis story, you must obtain the permission from the storyteller who told it to you. Not obtaining permission is a grave offence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always seek explicit permission from the originating storyteller/Elder before retelling; treat storytellers and their intentions with deference and follow community protocols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stories as truth and connection to ancestry
rubrics_metrics.description: Métis stories are not 'make-believe.' The Elders or Old People... believe them to be true. Stories have an undercurrent of truth and shouldn't be easily dismissed as myth or superstition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach narratives with humility and recognition of their truth-status within the community; avoid dismissive framing that reduces them to folklore or mere fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemporary adaptation and historical sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: The Métis Oral Tradition continues today in our print-based society, with stories being adapted into novels, poetry, art and film... this process has been greatly disrupted by societal pressures and forced assimilation policies such as residential schools and the Sixties Scoop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adapting stories into modern media, be sensitive to historical trauma, ongoing impacts of colonization, and the fact that many knowledge forms were interrupted; prioritize community-led adaptation and context.
